title: China Is Now the World's Top Car Exporter, but Its Automakers Haven't Finished Japan's Overseas Course
dek: China exported 4.41 million vehicles in 2023 to take the global top spot, yet from 2012 to 2020 its total exports were stuck at around 1 million a year for eight straight years. Japanese automakers' first foray into the US in the 1950s was a rout; they only turned it around on the back of the 1970s oil crisis — a crisis is an opportunity, but political risk matters as much as economic risk.
why: It uses 60 years of Japanese automakers' overseas history as a mirror for China today; the details of Toyota's and Honda's failures and comebacks are concrete, and offer a direct reference for understanding the political risks Chinese automakers face going abroad.
who: Founders and investors watching Chinese auto exports, geopolitical risk and the globalization of manufacturing, plus industry researchers who want to understand how Japanese automakers rose.
skip: After 1:15:59, the discussion of how global sales figures are counted can be skipped.

points.h: Eight years stuck at 1 million: not a product problem but a geopolitical one
points.body: From 2012 to 2020, China's total vehicle exports — including both fuel-burners and new energy vehicles — hovered around one million units. Zhang Junyi teases out three reasons. First, export destinations were concentrated: Iran was once the largest overseas market for Chinese automakers, and after US sanctions on Iran, in 2019 China exported not a single car to Iran, causing a major slump. Second, European and American regulations and technical requirements are complex and certification cycles are long. Third, sea and land transport capacity was limited, with tight slots and high prices — at one point Tesla booked entire ro-ro ships, leaving other automakers with orders they could not ship. Earlier still, in 2005 a Chinese model scored zero in a German crash test, which directly caused the first overseas push to fail.

points.h: The pandemic broke international supply, and Chinese cars filled the gap
points.body: After the pandemic began in 2020, international supply was disrupted and many overseas markets struggled to deliver vehicles; Chinese models, accepted by consumers for their practical and application value, became a major supplement to local markets. At the same time, the shipping capacity problem was gradually resolved and export certification completed, so exports scaled up as a matter of course. In 2021 they suddenly broke 2 million units, overtaking South Korea to become the world's third-largest vehicle exporter behind Japan and Germany; in 2022 they broke 3 million to overtake Germany; in 2023 they overtook Japan. Zhang Junyi repeatedly stresses one line: never waste a good crisis.

points.h: To fend off outsiders you must first settle things at home: an unstable domestic base means overseas setbacks
points.body: Zhang Junyi says the phrasing may not be quite right, but the meaning is this: for a company to live well and survive, it must live well and survive as a whole, and the overseas business is always attached to the domestic business. If the domestic base is unstable, overseas development will also suffer setbacks. He gives two counterexamples: Aiways had considerable early export volume, but after its domestic business stumbled, its international business gradually changed too; Great Wall, unable to sell domestically at the time because it could not obtain a license, instead developed in places like Russia and then turned back to the domestic market. But new energy vehicles are a scale-competition market, with the gap between leaders and laggards widening, and going straight overseas without a certain base volume is a huge challenge.

points.h: Toyota's first US foray: ugly, expensive cars nobody bought
points.body: In the 1950s Toyota's first attempt to export to the US met with a major setback. Japanese cars were compact, small and durable, completely at odds with the flashy, large, powerful and gas-guzzling design of American cars, and Americans found them ugly and unsuitable. Zhang Junyi breaks down the specific reasons: the US wanted large-displacement, large-body cars, while Japanese cars had insufficient horsepower and were small; Japanese roads were poor at the time, so the vehicles were designed for Japanese road conditions; on price, a Toyota model cost nearly 2,000 US dollars, equivalent to 67% of the average American wage at the time, so Americans could not afford it either; and more critically, the overseas strategy was simply immature, with neither the sales nor the service and maintenance market in place — with no parts supply, nobody dared buy.

points.h: The oil crisis gave small-displacement Japanese cars their opening
points.body: In the 1970s oil crisis, American cars were powerful but burned fuel heavily — gas guzzlers — and both sales and profits were hit hard. In the two crises GM's profit fell 50% and revenue fell 30%; Ford's profit contracted threefold, turning from positive to negative growth. Consumers could no longer afford to run big gas burners and wanted fuel-efficient cars, and Japanese cars seized the moment to enter the US market on the strength of their energy-saving attributes. This was Toyota's second overseas push. Zhang Junyi says: never waste a good crisis — a crisis is also an opportunity.

points.h: The Corolla weighed 950 kg; American cars weighed two tonnes
points.body: Toyota made concrete preparations for its second overseas push: models were developed in a direction American consumers could accept, manufacturing quality kept improving, and the Corolla went through many iterations. The most critical factor was fuel consumption — beyond aerodynamic design, vehicle weight had to be considered: at the time a Corolla weighed an average of 950 kg, while American cars of the same period were basically two tonnes, and a Cadillac's engine was essentially an 8.2-litre V8. In the 1970s the Corolla was generally about 400 to 1,000 US dollars cheaper than American cars. On overseas strategy, Toyota did market research, localized product adjustments, set up a sales company in the US, and had dealer networks on the West Coast and in the eastern Bay Area. Later, to avoid trade friction, it also built factories locally, and after the 1990s it invested overseas on a large scale.

points.h: In China, Toyota chased profit, not market share
points.body: Zhang Junyi points out that Japanese automakers consider potential political risk deeply when laying out their industries. What Toyota pursued in China was profit growth, without being overly aggressive about overall market share. Compare the figures: Volkswagen's share of the Chinese market reached 50% in 2019, BMW nearly 30%, Honda nearly 30%, while Toyota was basically 16%, and may be lower now. Toyota was thinking about what to do if potential political risk materialized, so it weighed profit growth against total volume growth more heavily. This is not just Toyota — Japanese and Korean companies mostly make this kind of strategic choice too.

points.h: Behind Toyota's recall case was a US-Japan auto war
points.body: In 2010 Toyota recalled about 2.3 million vehicles over the accelerator pedal issue, and Zhang Junyi sees this as something like a crisis war, even a conspiracy war. The backdrop: the 2008 financial crisis hit the US auto industry hard, while Toyota had already become global number one in 2007, and 2008 happened to be GM's centenary — GM lost the global number one spot to Toyota on its own hundredth birthday. After 2008 GM collapsed and had to rely on government subsidies, and then came the massive recall over Toyota's sudden acceleration, with Congress even demanding that Toyota's president appear at a hearing, turning the recall issue into a matter of form. But Zhang Junyi also says you cannot blame only the US government; this is also a historical warning: an automaker cannot coast on past glories, its products must pass muster, and it must meet the most basic moral and safety requirements.

quotes.text: Never waste a good crisis. When it comes to going overseas, political risk and economic risk are equally important.

Japan's resources are limited, and its market determines that if it does not go outward, it has no way out. This is actually a particularly interesting thing about Japan: its going overseas was in fact determined by geopolitics.

If technological development were entirely linear, the leader would keep leading as long as it did not make mistakes. But because technology has turning points, everyone has to make trade-offs, and different trade-offs produce different outcomes. The most important thing for a person is choice, not effort.

An automaker cannot coast on past glories. In the end, your product has to pass muster, meet consumer needs, and satisfy the most basic moral and safety requirements. If you fail to do that, you will ultimately be spurned by the market.

Those who can truly gain a foothold in a local market must rely on high-quality, premium products. Why could Japan gain a foothold in the US, to the point that it later competed so hard it turned Detroit into an empty, ghost town?
